idiom_name: pub struct with private fields + pub(crate) items and sealed traits
implementation_notes: Rust needs no pointer: a public struct may keep every field private, and pub(crate) or private items plus the crate boundary decide what is nameable, so the representation can change in a minor release without breaking callers - the API guidelines state this directly as 'structs have private fields'. What replaces the wrapper is privacy plus the constructor idiom: an associated new builds the value, methods expose behaviour, and where a hidden type would otherwise appear in a public signature you wrap it in a newtype or hand back impl Trait or Box<dyn Trait>; sealed traits (a public trait with a private supertrait) close a trait to downstream implementations. Keep a Box body only when the value is large, recursive or genuinely type-erased - the compiler already provides the firewall.
pitfalls: A public field is a permanent commitment: it pins the representation and blocks validation, and it cannot be made private again without a major version.

Hiding a type does not hide it from a public signature: a private type in a public API triggers the private_interfaces lint, so the hidden type must be wrapped as a newtype or erased behind Box<dyn Trait> or impl Trait - that is the only place the pointer-to-body shape legitimately reappears.

Cargo has no stable ABI between compiler releases: private fields protect source compatibility and semantic versioning, not binary compatibility, so every dependency upgrade still recompiles consumers.

variants.name: Opaque handle across an FFI boundary
variants.idiom_name: #[repr(C)] struct with a private field, Box<Foo> as Foo*
variants.implementation_notes: At an FFI boundary the opaque pointer is exactly the C idiom: a #[repr(C)] struct with at least one private field and no constructor can only be used behind a pointer, and Box<Foo> is ABI-compatible with Foo*, so foo_new() -> Box<Foo> and foo_delete(Option<Box<Foo>>) hand the foreign side a handle it cannot inspect. The Rustonomicon recommends a PhantomData<(*mut u8, PhantomPinned)> marker so the type is neither Send, Sync nor Unpin, and the Box documentation warns that only pointers produced by the global allocator may be turned into Boxes. RFC 1861's extern type is the intended future spelling but is not stabilised, so the private-field marker struct is the portable form today.
pitfalls: Turning an arbitrary pointer into a Box is undefined behaviour: Boxes must be aligned, non-null, and created by the same global allocator, and a Box asserts uniqueness over its contents.
The marker type exists for a reason - without it the handle becomes Send, Sync and Unpin, so callers may move or share a foreign pointer across threads and break the ownership contract.
extern type is the intended future form but unstable; adopting it later changes the type-level shape of the API even though the C ABI stays the same.
